newsitem.title: INDIA: Mother Teresa better, doctors to decide on test.
newsitem.headline: Mother Teresa better, doctors to decide on test.

text.p: Mother Teresa's doctors will meet on Thursday to decide if she is strong enough for a special X-ray test in her battle against a faltering heart, a member of the panel treating her told Reuters.
The ailing nun had a peaceful night, following an episode of chest pain and breathing difficulty on Wednesday, doctors at a heart clinic in India's eastern city of Calcutta said.
"She is better," said Dr Tarun Praharaj, one of the doctors treating the legendary missionary at Calcutta's B.M. Birla Heart Research Centre. "There was no discomfort last night."
Praharaj told Reuters the doctors would decide by Thursday afternoon if Mother Teresa was strong enough for an angiography they had put off after she complained of chest pain on Wednesday.
The test uses an X-ray and an opaque dye injected into the blood vessels to check for arterial blockage.
"We will again examine her this morning," Praharaj said. "After that we will decide the next step." The decision would likely be announced by 12.30 p.m. (0700 GMT) he said.
The 86-year-old missionary was moved to the clinic on Tuesday from the nearby Woodlands Nursing Home, where she was admitted last Friday with an irregular heartbeat.
Mother Teresa's heart problem worsened soon after, and her doctors delayed the test, expected to show if she needed surgery. It had originally been scheduled for Wednesday.
"She is quite unstable," Dr Praharaj said on Wednesday.
Members of the Missionaries of Charity, the religious order that Mother Teresa founded in 1949, prayed for her recovery.
"We are having prayers all over the world for her recovery," Sister Priscilla, the order's spokeswoman, said.
The charity, devoted to the poor, destitute and dying, has about 4,500 nuns in some 80 countries.
Britain's Independent newspaper reported on Wednesday that Mother Teresa had begged her doctors to let her die.
"She talked very openly about not wanting to live any longer," the Independent quoted Jim Towey, a former seminarian with Mother Teresa's Missionaries of Charity order, as saying.
"She's helped so many people to die that she can accept mortality much better than her doctors," Towey said.
Calcutta's Hindus, Moslems and Sikhs joined in prayers for the 1979 Nobel Peace prize winner.
"We are all praying and we believe she will be all right," said Mohammed Halim, an inmate of the order's Nirmal Hriday (Innocent Heart) home in Calcutta.
"She gave us shelter and saved us from a shameful death in Calcutta's streets. God will save her," he said.
Mother Teresa, known as the "Saint of the Gutters" for her work with the poor, was fitted with a heart pacemaker in 1989.
She has undergone coronary angiography twice -- in the United States in 1991 and at the Birla centre in 1993.
Each time she also underwent angioplasty, with surgeons inserting a balloon into an artery, and then inflating it to unblock the artery.
Praharaj said the X-ray would show if a third angioplasty was necessary. But he added that Mother Teresa had more severe health problems now than in 1993.
"Her irregular heartbeats, chest pain, and chest infection double the risk, but there is no alternative," Praharaj said.
"We have to go for an angiogram and angioplasty, or she could develop more critical problems, like total blockage of arteries or total heart failure."
Dr S.K. Sen, medical director of the Woodlands Nursing Home, said Mother Teresa had ischaemia, or hardening of the arteries. Her heart has failed several times since last Thursday.
